[Question]
I am a third-year business student. I entered this department as my parents wished, but the classes bore me. Taking photographs is far more enjoyable than looking at numbers. Lately I have been wondering whether to give up my major and study photography from scratch. But I have only one year left before graduating, so I hesitate. What should I do?

[Answer]
From your message it seems you have a lot on your mind. The first thing I want to say is that your present major is not useless. Even for someone who makes photography their job, the ability to plan and to manage money is essential.

So before you give up your major, I would advise you to try three things. First, take pictures steadily in the school photography club or in a class. Doing it as a hobby feels different from doing it as an assignment. Second, meet someone who works in photography and hear directly how they spend their day. Third, in the holidays, work as an intern at a company connected with photography. As you build up experience, you will come to know whether this work really suits you.

The important thing is that you do not have to decide your career all at once. It is not too late to change direction little by little according to what you try and feel.

**-다고요?** (3A): you check what the listener **has just said**. **-다니요?** (3B): you are shocked at it. **-다면서요?**: you heard it **earlier, from someone else**, and now bring it up with the person concerned — a friendly way to start a conversation.
V-다 보면 — if you keep doing it

If the action in the first clause **goes on for a while**, the second will **naturally come about**: 매일 연습하**다 보면** 실력이 늘 거예요 (if you keep practising every day, you'll improve). It attaches to the verb stem. The result is usually **-(으)ㄹ 거예요, -게 될 거예요, -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요, -아/어져요**.

It encourages: 살**다 보면** 좋은 날도 올 거예요. And it warns: 그렇게 공부만 하**다 보면** 건강이 나빠질 수도 있어요. The second clause is **not in the past** — for something that already turned out, use **-다 보니(까)** (unit 5): 하다 보니 익숙해졌어요.

A formal way to **say what something consists in**. The topic is an abstract noun — 장점, 단점, 문제, 특징, 차이점, 중요한 것 — and the content is a whole clause in the quoted form + **는 것이다 / 점이다**: 저의 장점은 끈기가 있**다는 것입니다** (my strength is that I persevere). 문제는 시간이 없**다는 점입니다**.

제 취미는 사진을 찍**는 것**입니다 — the topic *is* the action. 제 장점은 사진을 잘 찍**는다는 것**입니다 — the topic is explained by a **statement about a fact**. With 장점, 문제, 특징, 차이점, the statement form **-다는** is the natural choice. 것 is neutral; **점** stresses “the particular point”.
V-는 대로 — in the way that

The second action **follows the first exactly**: 제가 말하**는 대로** 따라 하세요 (repeat as I say). Something already done → **-(으)ㄴ 대로**: 들**은 대로** 썼어요 (I wrote it as I heard it), 책에 나**온 대로** 만들었어요. Something to come → 하고 싶**은 대로** 하세요 (do as you wish).

Attached straight to a noun, without a space: 약속**대로** (as promised), 계획**대로** (according to plan), 순서**대로** / 차례**대로** (in order, in turn), 사실**대로** (truthfully), 마음**대로** (as one pleases), 그**대로** (as it is), 예상**대로** (as expected).

[A] Using earphones
Warning: if you go on listening to loud music for a long time, your hearing may get worse. After listening for an hour, rest your ears for about ten minutes. In noisy places such as the underground you end up turning the sound up, so take particular care. Once hearing has got worse, it is hard for it to recover.

[B] Look ahead when you walk
Warning: if you go on looking at your phone while walking, there may be a serious accident. When you walk looking at your phone, you cannot properly see not only people coming towards you but cars either. Not only can you get hurt yourself, you can hurt other people too. Put your phone in your pocket when you cross the road.

Last winter I caught a bad cold. My throat stung so much that it was hard even to drink water. I had taken some medicine and was lying down when my grandmother brought me a cup of hot tea. It was ginger tea: ginger sliced thin, boiled for a long time, with honey added.

“In the old days the hospital was far away, so when we caught a cold we drank this and sweated it out.”

The ginger tea was hot and sweet. When I had drunk the whole cup, not only did my body warm up, my stinging throat seemed to ease a little too. My grandmother knows many folk remedies like this. When I have indigestion she gives me plum tea, and when my neck is stiff she lays a warm towel on it.

Of course folk remedies do not cure every illness. That time too my fever would not go down, so the next day I went to the doctor's and was prescribed medicine. The doctor told me to take the medicine, drink warm tea often and rest well.

Looking back now, I think what made me better was not only the medicine but my grandmother's kindness. Even now I make ginger tea when my throat hurts. But if I am not better after three days, I always go to the doctor's. That is because if you do nothing but put up with being ill, a small illness can become a big one.

Korean names a symptom as **the part + 이/가 + a describing word**: **눈이 침침하다** (eyes dim after a long day at the screen) · **목이 뻣뻣하다** (neck stiff — the back of the neck) · **목이 따끔거리다** (throat stings — the inside) · **속이 거북하다** (stomach heavy after too much food) · **속이 쓰리다** (stomach burns) · **가슴이 답답하다** (chest tight; also “I feel stifled”).

**붓다** — to swell (ㅅ drops: 부**어요**, 부**은** 발목, but 붓**고**) · **막히다** — to be blocked: 코가 막히다 · **가렵다** — to itch (ㅂ: 가려**워요**, 가려**운** 데) · **저리다** — to go numb with pins and needles: 다리가 저려요 · **어지럽다** — to be dizzy (어지러**워요**).

The prefix **과(過)-** means “past the limit”: **과로** (overwork) · **과식** (overeating) · **과음** (drinking too much) · **과속** (speeding) · **과소비** (overspending). Add 하다 for the verb: 과식**했더니** 속이 거북해요. The general word is **지나치다** — 지나친 흡연, 지나치게 많이 먹다 — and for overstraining yourself, **무리하다**.
**심하다** — severe: 기침이 심해요. **낫다** — to get better (ㅅ drops: 나**았어요**, 나**을** 거예요, but 낫**지** 않아요). **푹 쉬다** — to rest properly. A wish for a sick person: **빨리 나으세요**.

So … that: 어찌나 -(으)ㄴ지/는지; to the point that: -(으)ㄹ 정도로

The first clause says **how extreme** something is, the second what **came of it**: 길이 **어찌나** 막히**는지** 한 시간이나 걸렸어요 (the traffic was so bad that it took a whole hour). Adjective → **-(으)ㄴ지**: 바쁜지, 매운지. Verb → **-는지**: 먹는지, 우는지. Finished → **-았/었는지**: 피곤했는지. 얼마나 can replace 어찌나; **어찌나** sounds stronger and more spoken.

It reports **your own experience**, so the second clause is a statement — not a command or a suggestion. And compare 3B **얼마나 -(으)ㄴ지 몰라요**: that one simply exclaims (얼마나 추운지 몰라요), while **어찌나 추운지 + result** tells what the cold led to (…밖에 못 나갔어요).

**정도** = degree. **-(으)ㄹ 정도로** measures the main clause by an example: 눈물이 **날 정도로** 매워요 (hot enough to make your eyes water). At the end of a sentence: 너무 아파서 허리를 못 **펼 정도예요**. The example is often an exaggeration or an inability: 못 -(으)ㄹ 정도, -기 힘들 정도.
They combine naturally: 목이 **어찌나** 아픈**지** 침도 못 삼**킬 정도예요** (my throat hurts so much that I can't even swallow). Note **N도 못 V** — “can't even V”.

**참다** — to put up with pain, hunger, laughter: 아파도 참았어요. **엄살** — making more of a pain than it is: 엄살 부리지 마 (stop making a fuss). Telling a truly ill person 엄살이지요? is rude. **무리하다** — to push yourself too far.

If the present behaviour **continues**, something **bad** will follow: 그렇게 손톱을 깨물**다가는** 손 모양이 이상해질 거예요. It is 다가 (in the middle of) + 는. It usually starts with **그렇게 / 이렇게** and ends in a guess: **-(으)ㄹ 거예요, -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요, -겠어요**.

Both mean “if this goes on”. **-다 보면** (unit 1) is neutral and mostly encouraging: 연습하다 보면 잘하게 될 거예요. **-다가는** is **only for bad outcomes**: ~~연습하다가는 잘하게 될 거예요~~. After the past, **-았/었다가는** warns about a single act: 지금 나**갔다가는** 감기에 걸릴 거예요.

**Not only A but also B** — B adds to A in the **same direction** (both good, or both bad): 이 가게는 값이 **쌀 뿐만 아니라** 질도 좋아요. The second clause usually has **도** or **까지**. Past: 했**을 뿐만 아니라**. Do not join a plus and a minus — for that use -지만.
After a noun, **뿐** is attached: 어른**뿐만 아니라** 아이들도. After a verb or adjective it is a separate word: 예방**할 뿐만** 아니라. The short form **N뿐 아니라** is also used.

Written warnings start with **경고:** and use formal endings: **-(으)ㄹ 수 있습니다**, **-(으)십시오**, **-아야/어야 합니다**. Typical words: **지나친** 흡연 / 음주, **질병**에 걸리다, **예방하다**, **사고가 나다**. Spoken: 그러다가는 큰일 나요 (carry on like that and you'll be in trouble).

**어디가 불편하세요?** · **언제부터 그러셨어요?** · **열이 나거나 토하셨어요?** · **전에도 이런 적이 있으세요?** · On the phone to 119: **지금 계신 곳이 어디입니까?** · **혼자 병원에 가실 수 있겠습니까?**

In Korea **119** is the number for a fire or an **구급차** (ambulance) — **신고하다** is to call it in. The same number also gives medical advice round the clock: staff tell you which hospital or pharmacy is open and what first aid to give. A hospital's **응급실** (emergency room) sees patients at night.
**N만 V-(으)면** — whenever: 높은 데**만** 올라가**면** 숨이 차요 (whenever I go up high…) · **-(으)ㄹ 때마다** — every time · strong dislike: **…은/는 딱 질색이에요** (I can't stand…). Useful with 멀미가 나다, 먼지, 꽃가루가 날리다.

Beside ordinary hospitals Korea has **한의원**, clinics of traditional Korean medicine. The doctor feels your **맥박** (pulse) to judge your condition, and may give acupuncture (**침을 놓다** — the doctor; **침을 맞다** — the patient), moxibustion (**뜸**) or **처방하다** a herbal medicine (**한약**), which is traditionally simmered for a long time (달이다). Many people go for a stiff neck, a sore back or a sprain.

When some nouns form the second half of a compound, their first sound is tensed although the spelling does not show it: 손**가락** [손까락], 빵**가게** [빵까게], 손**등** [손뜽], 발**바닥** [발빠닥], 길**가** [길까]. So 가게 → [까게] in 반찬가게, 쌀가게; 바닥 → [빠닥] in 방바닥, 땅바닥.

A personal essay is written in the plain style: 걸렸**다**, 정도였**다**, 아니**다**, 간**다**, 때문**이다**. The writer is **나**, not 저. Quoted speech keeps the grandmother's own voice: 땀을 냈**단다** (= 냈다고 한다, a warm way an older person tells a younger one).
3B causative: 병을 **낫게 하다** = to make an illness better, to cure. 나를 낫**게 한** 것은 … = what made me better was… Likewise 귀를 쉬**게 하다**, 기분을 좋**게 하다**.
민간요법이 병을 **다** 낫게 하**는 것은 아니다** = folk remedies do not cure *every* illness. With 다, 모두, 항상, it denies only the “all” (3B: N(이)라고 다 … 것은 아니다).

Have you ever seen a game called 3x3 basketball? 3x3 is basketball with three players on each team. A game that friends used to play in the street has become an official event.

Compared with five-a-side basketball, 3x3 needs fewer people. A team is made up of three players on court and one substitute. The court is about half a five-a-side court, and only one basket is used. So both teams shoot at the same basket.

The playing time is different too. Five-a-side basketball is played in four periods of ten minutes, but 3x3 is played just once, for ten minutes. Yet even before the ten minutes are up, the game ends if one team reaches 21 points first. If the score is level after ten minutes, there is extra time, and in extra time the first team to score 2 points wins. The scoring is different as well: a basket from inside the line is worth 1 point, from outside the line 2.

The chief feature of 3x3 is its fast pace. The team that has the ball must attack within 12 seconds. Play does not stop even after a score, so the players have almost no time to rest.

The advantage of 3x3 is that it can easily be played with few people and in a small space. And because the game is short and fast, it is so gripping that spectators cannot take their eyes off it.

“Whether you do it or not (마나 = 말다)”: the result is the same, so doing it is **pointless** — or the outcome is **obvious without trying**. 이 옷은 얇아서 입**으나 마나**예요 (too thin to be any use). 이 경기는 해 보**나 마나** 우리가 이길 거예요 (we'll win — no need even to play).

① **-(으)나 마나예요** — on its own: 그 사람한테는 말하나 마나예요. ② a confident guess: **-(으)ㄹ 거예요, -(으)ㄹ 게 틀림없어요, -(으)ㄹ 게 뻔해요**. Very common: **보나 마나, 물어보나 마나, 해 보나 마나, 들으나 마나**. It is not used with a negative: ~~안 가나 마나~~.

Something **unexpected** happened and **caused** a result you did not want: 비가 오**는 바람에** 경기가 취소됐어요. 버스를 놓치**는 바람에** 지각했어요. The form is always **-는 바람에**, even though the event is past; the main clause is in the **past**.

① Verbs only — ~~바쁜 바람에~~ → 바빠**서**. ② No past marker — ~~넘어졌는 바람에~~ → 넘어지**는** 바람에. ③ No command or suggestion after it. ④ A planned, deliberate cause sounds odd — it is for things that **just happened**. ㄹ drops: 울다 → **우는** 바람에.

**아깝다** — so close, what a waste: 한 골 차이로 지다니 아깝네요. **아쉽다** — a pity, one wishes it were otherwise: 아쉽게도 우리 팀이 졌어요. **역전승** — winning after being behind; **역전패** — losing after being ahead. **자신만만하다** — brimming with confidence (often before a fall).

**Compared with N** — the standard of comparison: 서울**에 비해서** 제주도는 날씨가 따뜻합니다. 서 may be dropped: 다른 경기장**에 비해** 좌석이 넓다. It is more formal than 보다 and usually comes at the start of the clause. Also **N에 비하면** (if you compare with N).

When N belongs to the same subject, it means **for, considering**: 그 선수는 나이**에 비해** 체력이 좋아요 (good stamina for his age). 값**에 비해** 질이 좋아요 (good quality for the price). 실력**에 비해** 좋은 평가를 못 받아요 (rated lower than his ability deserves).

**씨름** is traditional Korean wrestling. Two wrestlers face each other in a round **모래판** (sand ring), each gripping the other's **샅바** — a strong cloth belt tied round the waist and thigh, one red and one blue. Using strength and **기술** they try to **쓰러뜨리다** the opponent: whoever first touches the sand with the knee or any part of the body above it loses. A smaller wrestler who **버티다** and waits for the other to **균형을 잃다** can beat a bigger one. Traditionally the champion's prize was a bull.
After the ending **-(으)ㄹ**, a following ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅈ is tensed: 이길 **것** [이길 껃], 갈 **곳** [갈 꼳], 할 **수** [할 쑤], 못 일어날 **정도** [이러날 쩡도], 넘어질 **줄** [너머질 쭐]. Hence -(으)ㄹ 거예요 [꺼예요], -(으)ㄹ게요 [께요].

My elder sister and I grew up in the same house, but our personalities are quite different.

My sister is a planner, whereas I tend to move without a plan. When we travel, she fixes the accommodation and restaurants a month ahead. I, on the other hand, pack my bag on the morning we leave. So when we travel together, we are bound to quarrel for the first two days.

We also spend money differently. When I get paid I save first, whereas my sister first buys what she wants. Her room is full of pretty things, while mine has nothing but a bed and a desk.

People sometimes say “that's because he's a man” or “that's because she's a woman”. But my friend Minho is more meticulous than my sister, and my sister's friend Daeun is more scatterbrained than I am. So one cannot but think that such differences come not from sex but from people being different.

These days we divide the roles when we travel. My sister makes the plans and I manage the money. Since we are good at different things, the result is satisfying when we do it together.

Last week, in Korean class, the twelve students in our class did a simple survey. The topic was “Are men and women good at different things?” This was not an experiment by experts but an activity we tried for fun in class.

First the teacher asked three questions: “Are you good at finding your way?”, “Are you good at doing several things at once?”, “Do you quickly notice how other people feel?” We answered each with “yes” or “no”.

Before the survey most of the students thought the result was obvious. They expected that the men would be good at finding their way, whereas the women would be good at doing several things at the same time. But the actual result was different. Three men and three women answered that they were good at finding their way. Only two of each said they were good at doing several things at once. Most said that when tasks come all at once, far from handling them calmly, they get flustered.

Of course nothing can be argued from the answers of twelve people. But in doing this activity I became aware of a stereotype I had been carrying. The person in our class who finds the way best is Sujin, and the one quickest to read a mood is Marco.

Thinking of people as divided by sex is convenient; on the other hand, it makes it easy to miss what a person is really like. I cannot but think that ability varies with the individual rather than with sex.

**계획성이 없다** — spends the whole salary at once, packs on the morning of the trip (↔ 계획성이 있다). **눈치가 없다** — misses every hint (↔ **눈치가 빠르다**; 눈치 is the sense for what others feel without being told). **고집이 세다** — won't change their mind (세다 = strong: 고집이 **세서**, 고집이 **센** 사람). **자존심이 강하다** — too proud to accept help.

**불만** — a grievance: 불만이 있다 / 많다, 그게 내 불만이야. **속상하다** — to be hurt and upset inside. **불평하다** — to grumble. **따지다** — to demand an explanation point by point (왜 늦었어요? 누구랑 있었어요?). **지적하다** — to point out what is wrong. **화를 내다** — to show anger.

**-스럽다** turns a noun into an adjective: “having the feel of N”. 걱정 → **걱정스럽다** (worrying), 자랑 → **자랑스럽다** (proud of), 당황 → **당황스럽다** (flustering), 사랑 → **사랑스럽다** (lovable), 만족 → **만족스럽다**, 부담 → **부담스럽다** (too much to accept comfortably), 자연 → **자연스럽다**, 갑작 → **갑작스럽다** (sudden), 실망 → **실망스럽다**, 고급 → **고급스럽다**.

-스럽다 is ㅂ-irregular: 스러**워요**, 스러**운**, but 스럽**게**, 스럽**습니다**. Compare **-답다**: N답다 means being a proper N that one actually is (학생**답다** — as a student should be), while N스럽다 means resembling N without being it: an eight-year-old who talks sensibly is **어른스럽다**; a grown-up who behaves responsibly is **어른답다**.

**반면** = the opposite side. The pattern sets two **contrasting facts** side by side: 이 집은 학교에서 가까**운 반면에** 지하철역에서 멀다. Adjective **-(으)ㄴ 반면에**, verb **-는 반면에**, finished action **-(으)ㄴ 반면에**, noun **N인 반면에**. 에 may be dropped. Between sentences: **그 반면에** / **반면에**.
① Two **different subjects** compared: 누나는 계획성이 있**는 반면에** 나는 없다. ② **One subject**, a plus and a minus: 이 일은 월급이 많**은 반면에** 쉬는 날이 적다. It is more formal than -지만 and -는데, and fits reports and essays.

수 (a way) + 밖에 없다 (there is none but): ① **there is no other way** — 등록금이 없어서 입학을 포기**할 수밖에 없었다** (I had no choice but to give up). ② **it is only natural, bound to be so** — 좋은 재료로 만들었으니까 맛있**을 수밖에 없다**. The reason usually comes first with -(으)니까, -아서/어서, -기 때문에.

Quoted form + 더니 (= -다고 하더니): “they said / I heard X, and now…”. ① The reality **differs** from what was said: 내일 돌려**준다더니** 일주일이 지나도 연락이 없어요. ② The reality **matches**: 비가 **온다더니** 정말 오네요. Past statement: 갔**다더니**; noun: 학생**이라더니**.

The same form quotes a proverb and then shows it **coming true**: 원숭이도 나무에서 떨어**진다더니** 경험이 많은 지혜 씨도 실수를 했어요. 시작이 반**이라더니** 벌써 반이나 했네요. The proverb's last word is put in the quoted form: 온다 → 온다더니, 찍힌다 → 찍힌다더니, 못 한다 → 못 한다더니, 반이다 → 반이라더니.

Culture: 떡 and 소 in proverbs

Many Korean proverbs feature **떡** (rice cake) and **소** (the cow). 떡 is made from rice and was eaten on **명절** (holidays) and other special days — a **귀한** (precious) treat; hence **그림의 떡**, **누워서 떡 먹기**. Korea was a land of **농사** (farming), and a cow did the heavy work in the fields, so it was a family's most valuable possession: **소 잃고 외양간 고친다**, **바늘 도둑이 소도둑 된다** (small wrongs, left alone, grow into big ones).

Before a consonant only one of the two is sounded. **ㄺ** → [ㄱ]: 맑다 [막따], 읽다 [익따], 읽지 [익찌]; before ㄴ it becomes [ㅇ]: 읽는 [잉는], 맑네 [망네]; but before ㄱ the ㄹ is kept: 맑게 [말께], 읽고 [일꼬]. **ㄼ** → [ㄹ]: 짧다 [짤따], 넓다 [널따], 얇다 [얄따], 여덟 [여덜]. Exception: 밟다 [밥따]. Before a vowel both sounds are heard: 읽어요 [일거요], 넓어요 [널버요].

Reading: local news told with proverbs

Korean headlines are short noun phrases without endings: **인기 공연 표 구하기, 하늘의 별 따기**. The proverb gives the reporter's judgement in three words. In the body it returns inside a quotation: “…”**라고 말했다** / “…”**면서** …. A news item answers who, when, where, what, why.

예매를 시작**한 지** 삼 분 **만에** 매진되었다 = sold out only three minutes after booking opened. **만에** stresses how short (or long) the interval was. Ticket words: **예매** (advance booking), **매진** (sold out), **표를 구하다** (to manage to get a ticket).

**에야** = “only then, not before”: 사고가 난 다음 날**에야** 공사가 시작되었다 (only on the day after the accident did work begin). It carries reproach: it should have happened sooner. Also 이제**야** 알았어요 (only now do I understand).

Last Saturday I followed a friend to a pansori performance. I didn't really know what pansori was, so to be honest I expected little. As it is singing in old-fashioned language, I was also secretly worried that it would be boring.

The stage was simpler than I had imagined. There was only a singer standing with a fan, and beside her a drummer sitting at his drum. No other instruments, no splendid stage set. “Two people are going to perform for two hours?” I thought.

But when the singing began, my mind changed. The singer would sing, then tell the story in speech, and in the funny scenes she used gestures too. Alone she became the father, the daughter and the boatmen. There were subtitles, so I had no trouble following the plot. It was quite astonishing that with one voice she showed both the wide sea and a sad parting.

More surprising still was the audience. Not only the drummer but the spectators too called out loudly in the middle of the singing: “Eolssigu!”, “Jota!” This is called chuimsae. At first I was taken aback, wondering whether one may make a noise during a performance. But seeing the singer's voice gain strength when she heard the shouts, I tried joining in quietly. It felt as if the stage and the seats became one.

In the scene where the daughter leaves for her father's sake, I found a lump in my throat before I knew it. When the performance ended, the audience clapped for a long time. Young or old, everyone was on their feet.

On the way home I thought: pansori is the very kind of performance you have to go and see for yourself. I was ashamed of having thought it would not live up to expectations.

**아리랑** is the **민요** (folk song) every Korean knows. It is not one song but a family: each **지역** (region) has its own tune and **가사** (words) — the most **널리** known is the Gyeonggi version, and others famous by name are 정선 아리랑, 밀양 아리랑 and 진도 아리랑. **옳다** — right, as it should be: 옳은 일, 네 말이 옳아. **그르다** — wrong (르-irregular: **글러요**, 그른 일). Together: **옳고 그름** (right and wrong), 옳은지 그른지 (whether it is right or wrong). 옳다 is about morals and correctness; for a correct answer in an exam say 맞다.

**논란이 되다** — people argue about it: 요즘 논란이 되고 있는 문제. **현실성이 없다** — it could not happen in real life. **앞뒤가 안 맞다** — the first part contradicts the second; it does not add up. **문제가 안 되다** — it is no problem. Stronger than all: **말도 안 되다** — “absurd!”

**배려하다** — to think of others first. **양해를 구하다** — to ask in advance for someone's understanding: 미리 양해를 구했어요. **불편을 주다** — to inconvenience. **방해가 되다** — to get in the way of what someone is doing: 공부에 방해가 돼요. **양심이 없다** — to do wrong without shame. Good **예의** (manners) matter most in a **공공장소** (public place).

**-질** after a tool means working with it: 가위 → **가위질**, 망치 → **망치질**, 걸레 → 걸레질; so too **양치질** (brushing teeth). After other nouns it names an act, often a disapproved one: 도둑 → **도둑질** (stealing), 손가락 → **손가락질** (pointing at someone: 손가락질을 받다 = to be blamed by everyone). And one that just happens to you: **딸꾹질** (hiccups — 딸꾹질이 나다). Used with 하다: 가위질을 하다.

It attaches straight to the stem (먹더라도, 바쁘더라도), to the past (늦었**더라도**) and to nouns (학생**이더라도**). It is very often introduced by **아무리** (however much) or **무슨 일이 있더라도** (whatever happens).

Both mean “even if”. **-아도/어도** is neutral and may describe a fact: 약을 먹어도 안 나아요. **-더라도** is stronger and more hypothetical — it suits advice, promises and firm opinions about what should or should not be done: 아무리 배가 고프**더라도** 도둑질을 하면 안 돼요.

보다 here means “to view”: **저는 …다고 봐요 / 봅니다** = “in my view, I consider that…”. It presents an opinion as a considered judgement, a little more formal than -다고 생각해요, and is the normal form in debate. The clause before it is in the quoted form: 중요하**다고** 봐요, 필요하**지 않다고** 봐요, 해야 **한다고** 봅니다, 문제**라고** 봐요.

Grant a point, then object: **그렇긴 하지만** … · **이해는 되지만** … · **아무리 -더라도** … 은/는 말도 안 돼요. Turn the question round: **…씨 같으면 그렇게 할 수 있겠어요?** (could you do that in his place?). Close: **그것 보세요** (there you are) · **그래서 저는 …다고 봐요**. One's angle is a **관점**; one's position, an **입장**.

**찬성하다** (to be for) ↔ **반대하다** (to be against): 저는 그 의견에 찬성해요. **의견** — an opinion. Useful nouns for the stories people argue about: **진심** (true feeling: 진심으로 사랑하다), **용기** (courage), **세대 차이** (generation gap), **안정적인** 직장 (a secure job), **몰래** (behind someone's back), **후회하다** (to regret).

One action is done **while the state left by another still holds**: 불을 켜 놓**은 채로** 잠이 들었어요 (I fell asleep with the light still on). 신발을 신**은 채** 방에 들어갔어요. The form is always **-(으)ㄴ 채**, whatever the tense of the sentence; 로 may be dropped. The state is usually one that **ought to have been changed first** — so the pattern often carries surprise or mild reproach.

① Verbs only, and verbs that leave a **state**: wearing, holding, opening, switching on, sitting, standing, leaning. ② Not with 가다 / 오다 as the first verb: ~~학교에 간 채로~~. ③ Do not confuse it with **-(으)면서** (two actions going on together): 음악을 들**으면서** 걸었어요 — but 이어폰을 낀 **채로** 걸었어요.

In 1401, in the first year of King Taejong of Joseon, a great drum called the **신문고** was hung at the palace. “The rose of Sharon has bloomed” is a typical game that Korean children love to play. I have heard that other countries too have games with a different name and different words to shout but a similar method. No equipment is needed, and it can be played anywhere there is open space. Any number of players will do, from three to twenty.

The method is simple. First one player is chosen to be “it”. “It” stands facing a wall or a tree, and the others stand behind a line some way off. While “it” shouts “The rose of Sharon has bloomed!”, the others walk little by little towards “it”. When the words end, “it” quickly looks round. If anyone is seen moving at that moment, that person is caught. A caught player must go and stand beside “it”, holding “its” hand.

This is repeated until somebody gets close and strikes the joined hands of “it” and the caught player; then everyone runs away to the starting line. “It” chases and catches a runner, and the one who is caught becomes the next “it”.

The game looks ordinary, but it is effective for building the strength to freeze and for balance. And since “it” sometimes says the words fast and sometimes slowly, it stays interesting to the end.

Speaker: Good day. I am going to give a presentation on the dialects of Korea. Since coming to Korea I have made friends from many regions. I became interested in this topic when I found that my friends' intonation and way of speaking differ by region.

Korea has a standard language based on the speech of Seoul, and every region has its dialect. For example, for “어서 오세요” (welcome) some people say “어서 오이소” in Gyeongsang, “어서 와유” in Chungcheong and “어서 오랑께요” in Jeolla. On Jeju they say “혼저 옵서예”. People commonly say that Gyeongsang speech has strong intonation and is short, and that Chungcheong speech is slow and soft. One also often hears that Jeolla speech is rich in expression and so sounds warm. Of course these are impressions people get, and even within one region the way of speaking differs from person to person.

Chair: Thank you for your presentation. Does anyone have a question?
Listener: You said that Gyeongsang speech sounds blunt; please explain with a concrete example.
Speaker: Certainly. A friend of mine from Gyeongsang doesn't make a long speech of thanks but says shortly, “됐다, 마.” At first I thought it meant he was angry, but it meant “it's all right”.
Listener: I should like to know the cause of dialects differing by region.
Speaker: I read in a book the explanation that in the old days nature — mountains and rivers above all — made it hard to travel between regions. So speech changed differently in each region.

On Jeju Island there are people called haenyeo. Haenyeo are women who go into the sea without equipment such as oxygen tanks and gather seafood — abalone and sea urchins above all. This work is called “muljil”.

On each dive a haenyeo holds her breath for about a minute and goes down to a depth of some ten metres. Coming back to the surface, she lets out the breath she has been holding in one long exhalation, and it makes a sound like a whistle. This sound is called “sumbisori”. To hear sumbisori on the shore means that a haenyeo has come up safely.

Haenyeo do not work alone. Because the sea is dangerous, several go in together and keep an eye on one another. How to dive and what to know about the sea are learnt not at school but within the community. An experienced senior takes a newcomer around with her and teaches her what is where and when to come out of the water. It is then, too, that one learns not to be greedy and stay under until one is out of breath.

Among the haenyeo there are grandmothers of over eighty. But their number has fallen greatly compared with the past, because it is hard work and young people who take it up are rare. The culture of the Jeju haenyeo became a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016. The haenyeo's way of life — taking from the sea only as much as is needed, working together and sharing together — has an interesting story to tell us who live today as well.

**대표적이다** — the best-known example of its kind: 비빔밥은 한국의 대표적인 음식이다. **공통점이 있다** — to share something ↔ **차이가 있다** — to differ: 나라마다 약간씩 차이가 있다. **전통을 지키다** — to keep a custom alive: 설날에 세배하는 전통을 지키고 있다. **영향을 받다** — to be shaped by something: 날씨의 영향을 받는다.

**흥미롭다** — it makes you want to know more (ㅂ: 흥미로**워요**, 흥미로**운**). **독특하다** — unlike anything else, hard to describe ↔ **평범하다** — ordinary, nothing special. **단순하다** — simple, with nothing complicated in it. **흔하다** — found everywhere (김 씨는 한국에서 흔한 성이다) ↔ **드물다** — rare.

**-별** after a noun means “classified by”: **지역별** (by region), **나라별** (by country), **나이별** (by age), **직업별** (by occupation), 학년별, 월별 (by month), 종류별. It is used as **N별로** + verb (지역별로 다르다) or **N별** + noun (나라별 대표 음식).

When you describe a people or a region, keep to what can be seen, and soften the rest: **-는 편이다**, **-다고 한다** (they say), **-다는 이야기를 들었다** (I have heard that…), **사람마다 다르다**. An impression of a whole group is never the truth about each person in it.

The **표준어** (standard language) is based on the speech of Seoul; each region has its **사투리**. They differ in **억양** (intonation), **말투** (manner of speaking) and words. For “welcome” you may hear 어서 **오이소** (Gyeongsang), 어서 **와유** (Chungcheong), 어서 **오랑께요** (Jeolla), **혼저 옵서예** (Jeju). People often describe how a dialect *sounds* to them — **무뚝뚝하다** (curt), **정겹다** (warm), **점잖다** (gentle) — but these are impressions of sound, not of character, and speakers differ.

A traditional Jeju house had no **대문** (gate with doors). Instead, three wooden **막대기** (poles) could be laid across the entrance between two posts: this is the **정낭**. The poles tell passers-by where the **주인** (owner) is. All three **걸려** 있으면 — the family is far away and will be gone some time. Two — they will be back within the day. One — they are close by and will return soon. None — someone is at home; come in. The poles kept wandering cattle and horses out, and the custom is remembered as a sign of trust between neighbours.

A **condition followed by a request, command, proposal or promise**: 소식을 듣**거든** 저한테도 알려 주세요 (if you hear news, let me know). 민수 씨를 만나**거든** 안부를 전해 주세요. 무슨 일이 생기**거든** 꼭 연락하세요. It attaches to the stem; past **-았/었거든**. The second clause is **not a plain statement**: it ends in -(으)세요, -(으)ㅂ시다, -(으)ㄹ게요, -겠습니다, -아/어야 해요.

**-(으)면** is the general “if” and can be followed by anything: 비가 오면 길이 막혀요. **-거든** is narrower: a real, expected situation + what the listener (or I) should do. So ~~비가 오거든 길이 막혀요~~ is wrong, but 비가 오거든 우산을 가져가세요 is right. Do not confuse it with the sentence-final **-거든(요)** that gives a reason — see lesson 4.

A **guess from what one observes**, in a formal or written tone: 요즘 스트레스가 많**은 듯하다** (she seems to be under a lot of stress). 어머니가 주무시**는 듯해서** 조용히 했어요. 3B **-(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다** — a guess from visible evidence, in speech. 3B **-(으)ㄹ걸요** — a light guess in reply to someone. 4A unit 4 **-(으)ㄹ 게 뻔하다** — a sure and usually unwelcome forecast. **-(으)ㄴ/는 듯하다** — a careful guess in writing: profiles, reports, reviews, news.

**-(으)ㅁ** turns a verb or adjective into a noun form, and **notes, memos, profiles and notices end their sentences with it**: 솔직하고 적극적**임**. 매일 노래 연습을 **함**. 첫 앨범을 **냄**. After a vowel **-ㅁ**, after a consonant **-음**; past **-았/었음**; noun **N임**; planned **-(으)ㄹ 예정임**; guessed **-(으)ㄹ 듯함**. ㄹ-stems add ㅁ to the ㄹ: 살다 → **삶**, 만들다 → **만듦**.

On a door: 회의 중**임** (meeting in progress). On a notice: 오늘 수업 없**음**. In a diary note: 친구 만**남**. 영화 **봄**. In an interview memo: 하루에 세 시간 공부**함**. It is not used in speech or in ordinary letters. The same ending makes nouns of feeling and action you already know: 기쁨, 슬픔, 웃음, 꿈, 삶, 잠.

How a programme note is built

① **What it is**, in one noun phrase without a verb: 소설 「…」을 원작으로 한 주말 드라마. ② **What it shows**: …-는 일을 **그린다**. ③ **Who is in it**: …이/가 주인공이다 · …역할을 맡아 주목을 받고 있다. ④ **How it is judged**: …다는 **평가를 받고 있다**. ⑤ **What to expect or do**: …-(으)ㄹ 듯하다 · …-아/어도 좋을 듯하다.
**원작** is the original — the novel or comic a drama or film is made from. 소설을 **원작으로 한** 드라마 = a drama based on a novel. Similarly N을/를 **바탕으로 한** N (based on N), N을/를 **중심으로** (centred on N).

**과정** = process (unit 3). **-는 과정에서** = “in the course of …ing”: 사소한 **갈등**을 **해결하는 과정에서** 가족의 의미를 생각하게 해 준다. **갈등** is conflict between people; **사소하다** means too small to matter; **진정한** N is the true N.
**드라마**, **예능** (variety), **다큐멘터리**, **퀴즈** 프로그램, 뉴스, 토론. People on a show are **출연자**; those at home are **시청자**, who may **참여하다** (take part) by phone. A quiz gives **상금** (prize money).
